Remember this distinction: bioinformatics technicians manage how data is produced, while Biologists determine what the results mean. One extracts data; the other interprets significance.

A common path is a bachelor's degree in life science or computer science, bioinformatics assistant, technician, senior technician, then core analyst.
This work suits people who write scripts, pay close attention to detail, and read scientific literature. If reading data correctly is your standard, you can build a steady career here.

Bioinformatics technicians do more than run workflows or process data. They build and operate analysis workflows around sequencing and omics data, clean and align data, investigate quality-control anomalies, and turn raw reads into interpretable answers that support research and diagnosis. The work suits attentive people who can remain focused on code.

paragraphs: In the morning, run workflows to generate intermediate files. In the afternoon, remove dirty data and investigate anomalies. Locate every script error, send results to researchers for interpretation, consult literature and code, and archive the work before leaving.

According to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS), about 5,000 bioinformatics technicians were employed in 2024. Employment is projected to rise to 5,200 by 2034, a net increase of about 200 jobs, with approximately 300 openings each year. Median annual pay is about $71,500 in 2026 (BLS OOH, 2026).

AI will not replace bioinformatics technicians, but it will automate standard analysis workflows. Pipelines run automatically and results receive initial screening, shifting technicians from executing workflows toward breaking down problems and interpreting anomalies. Pure execution faces displacement, while people who write scripts and interpret results become more valuable.

A score of 8/10, relatively high, means this occupation has relatively high AI exposure in data workflows. Systems absorb pipeline execution, while problem decomposition and interpretation still leave an essential role for people.

High exposure does not mean complete risk. Pure pipeline execution faces replacement, not roles built around problem decomposition. People who write scripts and understand biology become scarcer as technology advances, while technicians limited to clicking Run face the greatest pressure.
